why: The general definition follows from the words 'cost' and 'overrun'; the distractors are causes or unrelated problems, recognisably narrower.
Follows from what bottom-up estimating is: break down further until each piece is estimable, then aggregate.
Staying within a baseline is an ongoing control activity by definition; a one-off estimate cannot do it.
Fitting an outlay to a named accounting-cost label with no derivation path, and the item is broken — the key says current costs while its own explanation argues replacement costs.
Asks for the formula's shape, not a figure; value earned minus money actually spent follows from what the two terms mean and from positive-is-good.
Reading a ratio of value earned to cost spent — above one means more value than spend — and the index name rules out the schedule options.
Follows from what a management plan is for — how the area will be measured and controlled — versus what a deliverable or charter contains.
Lower accuracy follows from the method being a top-down proxy on a similar past project rather than detailed build-up.
Pure ITTO-row recall across four paired options; the input lists for adjacent cost processes are an arbitrary enumeration.
Each distractor describes a different cost process, and aggregating activity costs into a baseline is what budgeting means.
The ordering is forced by dependency — you cannot budget before estimating or control before a baseline exists.
